paragraphs.text: In many towns, the roads outside primary schools are jammed with cars twice a day. Parents drive for understandable reasons: they are short of time, the weather is bad, or they worry about traffic. Yet I believe more children could walk to school than currently do.

Walking gives children exercise at the start of the day, and teachers at our local school say pupils who walk arrive more ready to learn. It also teaches children to understand road safety, which they cannot learn from the back seat of a car.

I accept that walking is not possible for every family. Some children live too far away, and some parents must drive on to work. For them, parking a short distance from the school and walking the last few minutes is a sensible compromise.
Schools can help by creating walking buses, in which a group of children walks a set route with adult volunteers. Where these have been tried, the number of cars at the gate has fallen noticeably.

items.prompt: The writer thinks parents who drive their children to school have no good reason to do so.
The writer believes walking helps children understand road safety.
The writer thinks the council should build wider pavements near schools.
The writer accepts that some families are unable to walk to school.
According to the writer, walking buses have reduced the number of cars outside schools.
